content: Virola sebifera, commonly known as Ucuúba-do-Cerrado or red ucuuba, is a tree species belonging to the Myristicaceae family, native to Central and South America. Virola sebifera is a tall and slender tree that can grow up to 30 meters in height. Its leaves are simple in structure and can reach lengths of up to 30 centimeters. The tree produces small, unisexual flowers that are arranged in panicles. Its fruit is reddish in color and oval in shape. Differentiating individual Virola species, which number between 40 and 60, can be challenging due to their similarities. The bark of Virola sebifera contains high levels of tannins and psychoactive compounds, including dimethyltryptamine (DMT) and 5-MeO-DMT. Indigenous communities utilize the bark for treating various skin conditions. The seeds of the tree, when ripe, are rich in fatty acid glycerides, particularly laurodimyristin and trimyristin. Industrial Uses The seeds of Virola sebifera are processed to extract yellow, aromatic fats that have a scent reminiscent of nutmeg. However, these fats are prone to becoming rancid quickly. Industrially, the fats are used in the production of candles, soaps, and other fat-based products. The properties of Virola fat are comparable to those of cocoa butter and shea butter. Homeopathy A homeopathic remedy known as Myristica sebifera (abbreviated as Myris) is derived from the fresh, red sap of the tree's injured bark. Traditional Medicine In traditional medicine, the inner bark of Virola sebifera is utilized by shamans among indigenous Venezuelan communities. The bark is either smoked to alleviate fever or cooked to expel malevolent spirits.
